questions.question_text: Which of these correctly describes the graph of $y=(x+1)(x-7)$?

options.why: Read the intercepts straight off the factors without flipping their signs, giving $x=1$ and $x=-7$ and an axis at $x=-3$.
Correct intercepts, but used the $y$-intercept $-7$ as the vertex $y$-value instead of substituting $x=3$.
Did not flip the signs of the factors AND used the $y$-intercept $-7$ as the vertex $y$-value.

questions.solution_text:
Concave up (coefficient of $x^2$ positive).
$x$-intercepts: $x=-1$ or $x=7$.
Axis $x=\dfrac{-1+7}{2}=3$, $y=(4)(-4)=-16$, so vertex $(3,-16)$.

questions.question_text: Which of these correctly describes the graph of $y=x^2-4x+3$?

options.why: Factorised as $(x+1)(x+3)$, matching the $+3$ but not the $-4x$, giving roots $-1,-3$ and an axis at $x=-2$.
Correct intercepts, but used the $y$-intercept $3$ as the vertex $y$-value instead of substituting $x=2$.
Factorised as $(x+1)(x+3)$ with the wrong signs AND used the $y$-intercept $3$ as the vertex $y$-value.

questions.solution_text:
Concave up (coefficient of $x^2$ positive).
$x$-intercepts: $0=(x-1)(x-3)$, so $x=1$ or $x=3$.
Axis $x=2$, $y=(2)^2-4(2)+3=-1$, so vertex $(2,-1)$.

questions.question_text: Which of these correctly describes the graph of $y=-(x-2)(x+4)$?

options.why: Ignored the leading negative sign, so the graph was read as concave up and the vertex $y$-value came out as $(-3)(3)=-9$.
Read the intercepts straight off the factors without flipping their signs, giving $x=-2$ and $x=4$ and an axis at $x=1$.
Ignored the leading negative sign AND did not flip the signs of the factors when reading the intercepts.

questions.solution_text:
Concave down (leading coefficient negative).
$x$-intercepts: $x=2$ or $x=-4$.
Axis $x=\dfrac{2+(-4)}{2}=-1$, $y=-(-3)(3)=9$, so vertex $(-1,9)$.

questions.question_text: Which of these correctly describes the graph of $y=(x+2)^2-9$?

options.why: Did not flip the sign of $b$; the vertex $x$-value is $-2$, not $2$.
Read $c=+9$, missing the minus sign, so the vertex is above the axis and there are no roots.
Solved $(x+2)^2=9$ as $x=\pm 3$, forgetting to subtract $2$.

questions.solution_text:
Concave up (coefficient of $x^2$ positive).
Vertex form gives vertex $(-2,-9)$.
$x$-intercepts: $(x+2)^2=9$, so $x+2=\pm 3$, giving $x=1$ or $x=-5$.

questions.question_text: How many $x$-intercepts does the graph of $y=(x+5)^2$ have, and where is its vertex?

options.why: A perfect square touches the axis once; it does not cross at two points.
Did not flip the sign of $b$; the vertex $x$-value is $-5$.
A vertex sitting on the $x$-axis gives exactly one intercept, not none.

questions.solution_text:
$y=(x+5)^2$ is a perfect square, so $(x+5)^2=0$ gives $x=-5$ only.
The curve touches the $x$-axis at its vertex $(-5,0)$.

questions.question_text: Compared with $y=x^2$, how does the graph of $y=-2(x-1)(x+3)$ open?

options.why: Missed the negative leading coefficient, which makes it concave down.
Read $|k|=2$ as making it wider; $|k|>1$ makes it narrower.
Both the sign and the width comparison are read the wrong way.

questions.solution_text:
Expanding gives a leading coefficient of $-2$.
The sign is negative, so it is concave down, and $|-2|>1$, so it is narrower than $y=x^2$.

questions.question_text: Which of these correctly describes the graph of $y=3x^2-6x-9$?

options.why: After taking out the $3$, chose the factor pair $(x+3)(x-1)$ with the wrong signs, giving roots $-3,1$ and an axis at $x=-1$.
Correct intercepts, but used the $y$-intercept $-9$ as the vertex $y$-value instead of substituting $x=1$.
Chose the factor pair with the wrong signs AND used the $y$-intercept $-9$ as the vertex $y$-value.

questions.solution_text:
Factorise: $3x^2-6x-9=3(x^2-2x-3)=3(x-3)(x+1)$.
Concave up (leading coefficient positive).
$x$-intercepts: $x=3$ or $x=-1$.
Axis $x=1$, $y=3(1)^2-6(1)-9=-12$, so vertex $(1,-12)$.

questions.question_text: Which of these correctly describes the graph of $y=-x^2+6x-9$?

options.text: Concave down; touches the $x$-axis once at $(3,0)$; $y$-intercept $-9$
Concave down; crosses the $x$-axis at $x=3$ and $x=-3$; $y$-intercept $-9$
options.why: A perfect square gives a single touch point, not two separate roots.

options.text: Concave up; touches the $x$-axis once at $(3,0)$; $y$-intercept $-9$
options.why: Missed the leading negative sign, which makes the parabola concave down.

options.text: Concave down; touches the $x$-axis once at $(-3,0)$; $y$-intercept $-9$
options.why: Solved the perfect square with the wrong sign; $-(x-3)^2$ touches at $x=3$.

questions.solution_text:
$y=-x^2+6x-9=-(x^2-6x+9)=-(x-3)^2$.
Concave down (leading coefficient negative).
$(x-3)^2=0$ gives one touch point at $(3,0)$.
$y$-intercept: let $x=0$, $y=-9$.
